To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the rate of secretion during short depolarizing pulses is determined by a time-dependent increase in [Ca2+], (ii) the [Ca2+]-dependence of secretion can be described by a model of vesicle fusion in which vesicles undergo a priming process that is Ca2+-dependent, and (iii) [Ca2+] rises to only tens of micromolar and decays over tens of milliseconds in response to short depolarizations in chromaffin cell
the submembrane [Ca2+] in chromaffin cell exocytosis does not rise to hundreds of micromolars, as is the case at the synapse, but to a peak of less than 10 microM.
Ca2+ channels are not colocalized with secretory granules and that the submembrane [Ca2+] that triggers vesicle fusion is < 10 micro M.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying neurotransmitter release.
the mechanisms of exocytosis and the dynamics of the secretory response.
the time course of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Ca2+ channels are not colocalized with secretory granules in chromaffin and other neuroendocrine cells, but that the secretory response is triggered by a Ca2+ signal that is generated at the plasma membrane.

the time course and peak of the [Ca2+] signal that triggers secretion in neuroendocrine and other cells are slower and lower than in nerve terminals, and that this is because the vesicles are not colocalized with Ca2+ channels in neuroendocrine but not in nerve cells.

the Ca2+ concentration in the microenvironment surrounding the secretory vesicles is not as high as the one in the synaptic cleft, and that this is due to the different localization of Ca2+ channel and secretory vesicle in the two types of cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+ triggers exocytosis at chromaffin cell nerve terminals, and the Ca2+ signal is a transient, spatially restricted event.

the secretory response to Ca2+ is a function not only of [Ca2+] but also of [Ca2+], the time course of [Ca2+i], the time course over which [Ca2+] is elevated and the spatial distribution of Ca2+ sources relative to vesicles.
the Ca2+ signal for exocytosis is not as sharp and intense in chromaffin and perhaps other neuroendocrine cells as it is in synapses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the time course of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis can be used to estimate the kinetics of Ca2+ entry into a cell and the time course of [Ca2+] at the sites where Ca2+ triggers vesicle fusion.
Ca2+ is not an "all-or-none" switch that triggers secretion in chromaffin and other neuroendocrine cells.
the Ca2+ concentration that triggers exocytosis is lower in chromaffin than in synaptic vesicles.
